findings.title: Remove hardcoded production credentials
findings.body:
The production SQL Server password is committed to source. Anyone with repository access, or any leak of it, gets database credentials. `TrustServerCertificate=True` also disables certificate validation, which allows MITM.

Suggestion: Load the connection string from configuration or a secret store (e.g. IConfiguration / Key Vault), rotate the leaked password, and drop TrustServerCertificate=True.
findings.label: defect:secret

findings.title: Stop mutating a shared Dictionary from Parallel.ForEach
findings.body:
Multiple threads read and write the static `Dictionary` concurrently. That corrupts its internal state (possible infinite loops or exceptions), and the read-modify-write loses updates, so totals are silently wrong. Because the field is static, the state is also shared across all instances and imports.

Suggestion: Use a ConcurrentDictionary with AddOrUpdate(customer, total, (_, old) => old + total), or aggregate sequentially / via a thread-local reduction.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Generate reset tokens from a CSPRNG
findings.label: defect:md5

findings.title: Handle a missing order instead of dereferencing null
findings.label: defect:nullderef

findings.title: Return Task instead of async void
findings.body:
With `async void`, callers cannot await completion or observe failures. Any exception (bad CSV, failed HTTP call, parse error) is rethrown on the synchronization context and can crash the process.

Suggestion: public async Task ImportAsync(string csvPath, CancellationToken ct = default)
findings.label: defect:asyncvoid

findings.title: Avoid new HttpClient per call and blocking .Result
findings.body:
A new HttpClient on every call (once per CSV row) exhausts sockets. Blocking on `.Result` ties up thread-pool threads inside Parallel.ForEach and risks deadlocks. There is also no caching, so the same rate is fetched for every row.

Suggestion: Inject a shared HttpClient (IHttpClientFactory), make the method async, and cache rates per currency.
findings.label: defect:dispose

findings.title: Fix off-by-one in window bound
findings.body:
The loop condition `i <= start + size` returns `size + 1` items. There is also no validation of negative `start` or `size`: a negative `start` throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException, and a negative `size` makes the List constructor throw.

Suggestion: for (var i = start; i < start + size && i < items.Count; i++)
findings.label: defect:offbyone

findings.title: Dispose the StreamReader
findings.body:
The StreamReader is never disposed, so the file handle leaks until finalization. This can lock the file on Windows.

Suggestion: using var reader = new StreamReader(csvPath);
findings.label: defect:dispose

findings.title: Parse decimals with invariant culture
findings.body:
`decimal.Parse` uses the current culture. On servers with a comma decimal separator, values like "12.50" are misread or rejected.

Suggestion: decimal.Parse(cols[2], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)
findings.label: valid

findings.title: URL-encode the currency parameter
findings.body:
`currency` comes from untrusted CSV input and is interpolated unescaped into the query string. This allows query parameter injection against the rate API.

Suggestion: $"https://rates.example.com/latest?base={Uri.EscapeDataString(currency)}"
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Race Condition
findings.body:
`Parallel.ForEach` updates the static `Dictionary` `TotalsByCustomer` from multiple threads with a read-modify-write. `Dictionary` is not thread-safe, so concurrent rows can lose updates, corrupt the dictionary, or throw. Any CSV large enough to run rows in parallel can trigger this, especially when several rows share a customer.

Related problems in the same method:
- `async void` means callers cannot await completion. Exceptions from a missing file, malformed rows (`cols[3]` out of range, `decimal.Parse`), or HTTP failures in `ToUsd` go unobserved or crash the process.
- `StreamReader` is never disposed, so the file handle leaks.
- Each parallel row makes a blocking HTTP call through `RateService.ToUsd`. It creates a new `HttpClient` per call and blocks with `.Result`, which risks socket exhaustion and thread-pool starvation.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Off-by-one
findings.body:
The loop condition `i <= start + size` returns `size + 1` items whenever enough items exist. For example, `Window(items, 0, 10)` returns 11 elements. Use `i < start + size`.

A negative `start` also throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` from the indexer. A negative `size` throws from the `List` constructor. Unlike `Page`, neither argument is validated.
findings.label: defect:offbyone

findings.title: Null Dereference
findings.body: `FirstOrDefault` returns null when the customer has no order with `orderId`. `order.Total` then throws `NullReferenceException`. Any unknown or mismatched order id causes this. Handle the not-found case explicitly, for example by returning null or a 404, or by throwing a meaningful exception.
findings.label: defect:nullderef

notes: SQL injection: In `OrdersController.CountMatching`, `customerPrefix` is concatenated directly into the SQL text. An input like `x' OR 1=1; DROP TABLE orders; --` lets an attacker run arbitrary SQL. Use a parameter instead, for example `LIKE @prefix` with the value `prefix + "%"`, and escape LIKE wildcards if needed.

Sensitive information exposure: `src/Data/Db.cs` hardcodes the production SQL Server credentials (`User Id=shop_app;Password=Sh0p!Prod#2026`) in source. It also sets `TrustServerCertificate=True`, which disables certificate validation and enables MITM. The credential should be rotated and loaded from configuration or a secret store.

Insecure password reset token: `PasswordHasher.ResetToken` computes MD5 of `email + yyyyMMdd`, with no secret or randomness. Anyone who knows a user's email can compute that day's valid token and reset the password, which allows account takeover. Use a cryptographically random token (`RandomNumberGenerator`) stored server-side with an expiry and single use, or an HMAC with a server secret.

findings.title: Production database credentials hardcoded in source
findings.body:
The connection string commits the production host, user and password to source control. Anyone with repo access, or any leaked build artifact, gets prod DB access. It also cannot be rotated without a code change, and it sets TrustServerCertificate=True, which disables TLS validation and allows MITM.

Suggestion: Remove it and rotate the password now. Load the connection string from configuration, environment variables or a secret manager, and drop TrustServerCertificate.

findings.title: Unsynchronized Dictionary mutated from Parallel.ForEach
findings.body:
The static Dictionary is read and written from multiple threads. Dictionary is not thread-safe, so this causes lost updates, corrupted internal state and possible exceptions or infinite loops. The read-modify-write is also not atomic. Because the dictionary is static, it is shared across all instances and requests.

Suggestion: Use ConcurrentDictionary with AddOrUpdate, or aggregate per-thread and merge. Better, drop Parallel.ForEach here.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Predictable password-reset token (MD5 of email + date)
findings.body:
The token is MD5(email + today's date) with no secret and no randomness. Anyone who knows a user's email can compute it and reset that account's password, which allows account takeover. It is also not single-use and does not expire, since it is valid for the whole day and can be recomputed at any time.

Suggestion: Generate Convert.ToHexString(RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(32)), store only its hash with an expiry and the user id, and invalidate it after use.
findings.label: defect:md5

findings.title: FirstOrDefault on a possibly-struct Order, then dereferenced
findings.body:
If no order matches, `FirstOrDefault` returns default. When Order is a reference type or record class, `order.Total` throws NullReferenceException. When it is a struct, the method silently returns 0 for a missing order. Either way, a missing order is not handled and callers get a crash or a wrong total.

Suggestion: var order = found.FirstOrDefault(o => o.Id == orderId); if (order is null) throw new KeyNotFoundException(...); (or return decimal?).
findings.label: defect:nullderef

findings.title: async void method loses exceptions and cannot be awaited
findings.body:
`async void` means callers cannot await completion or observe errors. Any exception (a bad CSV row, an I/O error) is raised on the synchronization context or thread pool and can crash the process. TotalFor can be read before the import finishes.

Suggestion: Change it to `public async Task ImportAsync(string csvPath, CancellationToken ct = default)`.
findings.label: defect:asyncvoid

findings.title: Unvalidated CSV parsing and a blocking network call per row
findings.body:
`Split(',')` with direct indexing throws IndexOutOfRange on short rows. It also breaks on quoted fields, and decimal.Parse uses the current culture. Each row calls rates.ToUsd, which makes a blocking HTTP request for every non-USD row inside parallel workers, which exhausts the thread pool. An exception inside Parallel.ForEach surfaces as an AggregateException, and in an async void method it is unobservable.

Suggestion: Parse with a CSV library and decimal.TryParse(..., CultureInfo.InvariantCulture). Cache rates per currency before the loop.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: New HttpClient per call and blocking .Result
findings.body:
Creating an HttpClient per call exhausts sockets and ignores DNS refresh, and it is never disposed. `.Result` blocks the thread, risking thread-pool starvation or deadlocks under a synchronization context. There is no timeout, status check or caching, and the currency value is interpolated into the URL without escaping.

Suggestion: Inject a shared HttpClient or IHttpClientFactory, make the method async, cache rates, and use Uri.EscapeDataString(currency).
findings.label: defect:dispose

findings.title: Off-by-one in Window loop returns size+1 items; no validation
findings.body:
The condition `i <= start + size` includes index start+size, so up to size+1 items are returned. A negative `start` makes `items[i]` throw ArgumentOutOfRange. A negative `size` makes the `List<T>(size)` constructor throw. `start + size` can also overflow.

Suggestion: for (var i = Math.Max(start, 0); i < items.Count && i < start + size; i++), and validate size >= 0.
findings.label: defect:offbyone

findings.title: Controller issues raw SQL over a shared DbConnection
findings.body:
The controller now takes a DbConnection and runs queries itself, bypassing OrderRepository. This splits data access across layers. It also shares one connection with the repository, which can fail if a reader is open on it.

Suggestion: Move CountMatching into OrderRepository and keep the controller free of DbConnection.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: StreamReader is never disposed
findings.body:
The reader is not wrapped in `using`, so the file handle leaks if an exception occurs and is held until finalization otherwise.

Suggestion: await using var reader = new StreamReader(csvPath); or `using var`.
findings.label: defect:dispose

findings.label: defect:sqli

findings.title: Predictable Reset Token
findings.body: The reset token is `MD5(email + yyyyMMdd)`. Both inputs are known or guessable, so an attacker can compute the token for any email and reset that user's password without access to the mailbox. Use a cryptographically random token (e.g. `RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(32)`), store a hash of it server-side, and give it an expiry.
findings.label: defect:md5

findings.body: A production DB host, user and password are committed in source. Anyone with repo access gets production credentials, and they remain in git history. Load them from configuration or a secret store and rotate this password.

findings.title: Surrogate pairs are split by p[0]
findings.body:
`p[0]` takes a single UTF-16 code unit, so names starting with a character outside the BMP produce a lone surrogate. The parts are never empty because RemoveEmptyEntries is used, so there is no crash.

Suggestion: Use `char.ConvertFromUtf32` with `Rune.GetRuneAt`, or take the first text element via StringInfo.

findings.title: Remove eval of caller-supplied formula
findings.body:
`eval(formula)` runs arbitrary JavaScript. If a formula comes from user input, an attacker gets code execution in the process.

Suggestion: Use a safe expression parser (e.g. a restricted arithmetic parser or a library like mathjs's `evaluate` with a limited scope) instead of eval.

findings.title: Remove hardcoded live API token
findings.body:
A live payments token is committed to source. Anyone with repository access can read it, and it will stay in git history.

Suggestion: Load it from the environment or a secret manager, e.g. `process.env.PAYMENTS_API_TOKEN`, and rotate the leaked token.
findings.label: defect:secret

findings.title: Block prototype pollution in mergeSettings
findings.body:
Keys like `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` from untrusted JSON are merged recursively. With `__proto__`, `target[key]` resolves to Object.prototype, so an attacker can pollute every object in the process.

Suggestion: Skip dangerous keys: `if (key === "__proto__" || key === "constructor" || key === "prototype") continue;` and use `Object.hasOwn` checks or null-prototype objects.
findings.label: defect:protopollution

findings.title: Avoid shell command injection in exportReport
findings.body:
`name` is concatenated into a shell command string. A name like `x; rm -rf ~` runs arbitrary commands.

Suggestion: Use `execFileSync("pdf-render", ["--out", "/tmp/reports", `${name}.pdf`])` and validate `name` against a strict pattern.
findings.label: defect:cmdinj

findings.title: Await or handle the saveAudit promise
findings.body:
`saveAudit` is async but `promote` neither awaits it nor handles its result. A rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection, and the audit may be lost while the promotion still succeeds.

Suggestion: Make promote async and `await saveAudit(...)`, or attach a `.catch` that logs or handles the failure.
findings.label: defect:floating

findings.title: Fix off-by-one loop bound
findings.body:
`i <= list.length` reads `list[list.length]`, which is undefined, so `.name` throws a TypeError on every call.

Suggestion: for (let i = 0; i < list.length; i++) — or `return list.map(u => u.name);`
findings.label: defect:offbyone

findings.title: Fix check-then-act race in reserveUsername
findings.body:
Two concurrent calls with the same name can both pass `has` before either reaches `add`, because of the await in between. Both then return true and the same username is reserved twice.

Suggestion: Add the name to `reserved` before awaiting, and remove it if the profanity check fails; or track pending reservations separately.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Fail closed when WEBHOOK_SECRET is missing
findings.body:
The secret defaults to an empty string. Anyone can then compute a valid HMAC with the empty key and forge webhook signatures.

Suggestion: Throw at startup if `process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset or empty.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Use constant-time signature comparison
findings.body:
`===` on the hex digests can leak timing information an attacker could use to recover a valid signature.

Suggestion: const a = Buffer.from(expected, "hex"); const b = Buffer.from(signature, "hex"); return a.length === b.length && timingSafeEqual(a, b);
findings.label: defect:timing

findings.title: Remove catastrophic backtracking from email regex
findings.body:
`^([a-zA-Z0-9]+\.?)+@` nests quantifiers over the same characters. A long alphanumeric string with no '@' causes exponential backtracking, which is a ReDoS risk.

Suggestion: /^[a-zA-Z0-9]+(\.[a-zA-Z0-9]+)*\.?@example\.com$/
findings.label: defect:redos

findings.title: Await fetchProfile inside try
findings.body:
`return fetchProfile(id)` without `await` lets a rejection escape the try/catch. The catch never runs, and loadProfile rejects instead of returning undefined.

Suggestion: return await fetchProfile(id);
findings.label: defect:returnawait

findings.title: Off-by-one
findings.body: The loop condition `i <= list.length` reads one past the end of the array. `list[list.length]` is `undefined`, so `.name` throws a TypeError. `displayNames` fails on every call, including with an empty array. Use `i < list.length` or `list.map(u => u.name)`.
findings.label: defect:offbyone

findings.title: Race Condition
findings.body: `reserveUsername` checks `reserved.has(name)`, awaits `checkProfanity`, and only then adds the name. Two concurrent calls with the same name both pass the check before either adds it, so both return `true` and the same username is reserved twice. Reserve the name before the `await` and roll back if the check fails, or track in-flight reservations.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Command Injection
findings.body: `name` is concatenated into a shell command and run with `execSync`. A value like `x; rm -rf ~` or `$(curl evil|sh)` runs arbitrary commands. Use `execFileSync("pdf-render", ["--out", "/tmp/reports", `${name}.pdf`])` and validate or sanitize `name`, which also blocks path traversal.
findings.label: defect:cmdinj

notes: Sensitive information exposure: `src/config.ts` hardcodes a live payments token (`PAYMENTS_API_TOKEN = "tok_live_..."`) in source. It should be revoked and loaded from a secret store or environment variable.
Code injection: `evaluate` in `src/calc.ts` passes `formula` directly to `eval`. Any untrusted input can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Node process.
Command injection: `exportReport` in `src/export.ts` builds a shell command from `name` (see key issue).

Prototype pollution: `mergeSettings` recursively merges arbitrary keys without blocking `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype`. Input such as `JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}')` pollutes `Object.prototype`.

Weak webhook authentication: `SECRET` falls back to `""` when `WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset. Anyone can then compute a valid HMAC and forge webhooks. The signature is also compared with `===`, which is not constant-time. Fail closed when the secret is missing and use `crypto.timingSafeEqual`.

ReDoS: the regex `^([a-zA-Z0-9]+\.?)+@example\.com$` in `isValidEmail` has nested quantifiers. A long alphanumeric string that fails to match, e.g. `"a".repeat(40) + "!"`, causes catastrophic backtracking and blocks the event loop.

findings.title: Waiting for both directions can hang forever and leak connections
findings.body:
Previously the first finished copy returned, and the deferred Close calls tore down both sockets, unblocking the other copy. Now handleTCP blocks until both copies end.

If either conn is not a HalfCloser, finishing one direction never signals the peer. The other io.Copy can then block indefinitely. Examples: a clientConn that is not a TCPConn, or a dialer returning a non-half-closable conn.

Even with half-close, a backend that does not close its side after receiving FIN keeps the relay goroutines and both FDs alive indefinitely. Many servers behave this way, ignoring EOF while idle.

A copy that fails with an error (e.g. a reset) should also tear down the whole connection, not wait for the other direction.

Suggestion: Only wait for the second direction when both conns support half-close. If a copy returns a non-nil error, close both conns immediately. Consider an idle timeout after the first direction completes.

findings.title: Unsynchronized readClosed flag
findings.body:
`readClosed` is written in CloseRead and read in Read without synchronization. CloseRead is typically called while another goroutine may be blocked in or entering Read, so this is a data race the race detector will flag. The guard is also redundant once the underlying conn's read side is shut down.

Suggestion: Use an atomic.Bool for readClosed, or drop the flag and rely on the underlying conn's CloseRead semantics.

findings.title: Possible Hang
findings.body:
`handleTCP` now waits for both copy goroutines before returning, so the deferred `srv.Close()` runs only after both finish. When one direction ends, only a half-close is propagated. The other `io.Copy` stays blocked until that peer closes its side.

If either conn is not a `nettype.HalfCloser`, nothing unblocks the second copy. This happens with a custom `Server.Dialer` returning a non-TCP conn, or with `connWithOneByte` wrapping a non-TCP conn, where the methods are silent no-ops. findings.title: Response body leaked when retrying on a retryable status in Open
findings.body:
When `client.Do` succeeds with a retryable status (now 429, 500, 502, 503, 504 or 509) and `err` is nil, the closure returns `true, nil`. The pacer calls the closure again and `res` is overwritten without closing the previous `res.Body`. Each retry leaks a connection and body, which blocks keep-alive reuse. Before this change only 429 triggered this path. The retry set is now much broader, so the leak is more likely to occur, and 5xx bodies can be large. The same happens in the presigned-URL download retry at line 924.

Suggestion: Before returning true, drain and close the body, e.g. `if retry := fserrors.ShouldRetryHTTP(res, retryErrorCodes); retry { _ = res.Body.Close(); return true, fmt.Errorf("retryable status %d", res.StatusCode) }`.

findings.title: Response body leak on retry

If retries are exhausted, the pacer returns a nil error, and the caller then treats the 5xx response as a successful download. Close the body before returning retry=true, and return an error carrying the status so exhausted retries fail.

findings.title: Wrapper hides optional host interfaces other than RegisterZPages
findings.body:
`hostWrapper` embeds the `component.Host` interface. Embedding an interface promotes only that interface's methods (`GetExtensions`), plus the explicitly added `Report` and `RegisterZPages`. Any other method the concrete host exposes is no longer reachable by type assertion. Before this change, extensions received the concrete `graph.Host` directly. An extension that probes for another capability, such as an existing or future `GetFactory`-style or module-info accessor, will now silently fail its assertion and fall back or misbehave. This makes the wrapper a fragile allow-list.

Suggestion: Audit the methods on `graph.Host` and forward each optional one explicitly. Alternatively, document that only `RegisterZPages` is supported and add a test asserting the forwarded set. Consider adding a compile-time check that `hostWrapper` satisfies each optional interface `graph.Host` implements.

findings.title: Hidden host capabilities
findings.body:

Extensions find these capabilities with type assertions, so they would now fail. Examples include `GetFactory` (`hostcapabilities.ComponentFactoryProvider`) and `GetModuleInfos` (`hostcapabilities.ModuleInfo`). Extensions that use them, such as an OpAMP-style extension reporting module info, would silently lose that functionality.

Fix: forward these interfaces too, the same way `RegisterZPages` is forwarded. Alternatively, build the wrapper dynamically so it preserves the underlying host's interfaces. Add tests asserting those capabilities still pass through.

findings.title: A throwing thenable in `pump` deadlocks the iterator
findings.body:
`pump` runs inside a promise executor or a `.then` callback. If the `chunk.then` getter or the `then` call throws, the exception only rejects the executor or derived promise, which nobody observes. The request's `resolve`/`reject` are never called and `inFlight` remains `true`. That request and every queued one hang forever, and the error may also surface as an unhandled rejection.

Suggestion: Wrap the `then` lookup and call in try/catch. On a throw, set `inFlight = false`, call `settleError(err, reject)` and then `drain()`.

findings.title: `chunk.then` throws for undefined object-mode chunks
findings.body:
In objectMode, `readableAddChunk` accepts `undefined` (only `null` means EOF), so `stream.read()` can return `undefined`. The new code reads `chunk.then` on that value and throws a TypeError synchronously out of `next()` (and out of `pump`). The previous async generator simply yielded `undefined`. This is a regression for any stream that pushes `undefined`. The same access in `pump` (line 1506) throws inside a promise callback, which leaves the request pending forever.

Suggestion: Guard the access: `const then = (chunk !== undefined && chunk !== null && (typeof chunk === 'object' || typeof chunk === 'function')) ? chunk.then : undefined;`

findings.title: `next()` returns whatever a user `then` returns
findings.body:
The fast path returns `FunctionPrototypeCall(then, chunk, ...)` directly. For a non-native thenable, `then` may return `undefined` or a non-promise, so `next()` breaks the iterator protocol and `for await` throws. If `then` throws synchronously, the exception escapes `next()` synchronously and `inFlight` stays `true` forever. Every later `next()`, `return()` or `throw()` is then queued and never settled, so the consumer hangs.

Suggestion: Wrap it in a native promise: `return new Promise((resolve, reject) => { try { FunctionPrototypeCall(then, chunk, (v) => resolve(onChunkFulfilled(v)), (e) => { try { onChunkRejected(e); } catch (x) { reject(x); } }); } catch (e) { inFlight = false; settleError(e, reject); if (queue !== null) drain(); } });`

findings.title: Queued requests can settle before the current one
findings.body:
`onChunkFulfilled` calls `drain()` before returning, and only the return value settles the outer promise (the promise returned by `then`). Queued `next()` requests resolved synchronously inside `drain` therefore settle before the request that preceded them. That breaks the in-order settlement the queue is meant to guarantee. `pump` avoids this by calling `resolve` before `drain`.

Suggestion: Settle the current request first, e.g. by wrapping it in an explicit `new Promise` and calling `resolve` before `drain()`, as `pump` does.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Fast path duplicates `pump` and its error handling
findings.body:
`next()` reimplements the read, thenable, error and EOF logic that `pump`/`processNext` already contain, using different callbacks (`onChunkFulfilled`/`onChunkRejected` versus inline closures). The two copies already differ in settlement ordering and in how a thrown `then` is surfaced. Every future fix has to be made twice.

Suggestion: Route the fast path through a shared helper that both `next()` and `pump` call, keeping one synchronous-shortcut branch.

findings.title: Non-promise thenables
findings.body:
On the fast path for a thenable chunk, `next()` returns whatever `chunk.then(...)` returns. Native promises return a promise, so they work. A spec-compliant custom thenable such as `{ then(res) { res(1) } }` returns `undefined` (or any non-promise value), so `next()` stops returning a promise. `for await` then fails with "Iterator result undefined is not an object".

The old async generator awaited any thenable correctly. A fix is to wrap the call, for example `new Promise((res, rej) => then.call(chunk, res, rej))`, or to resolve the value through a native promise before chaining.

findings.title: Sync throw/hang
findings.body:
This affects both the `chunk.then` getter and the `then` call itself.

- **Fast path:** if either throws, `next()` throws synchronously instead of returning a rejected promise. `inFlight` has already been set to `true`, so every later `next()`/`return()`/`throw()` is queued forever and the stream is never finalized or destroyed.
- **Waiting path (`pump()`):** the same throw happens inside a `.then` callback. It becomes an unhandled rejection, and the caller's `next()` promise never settles.

The old generator caught this in its `try` block, which set the error and destroyed the stream. The throw should be caught and routed through `settleError`/`onChunkRejected`.

findings.title: Multi-settling thenable
findings.body:
In `pump()`, the callbacks passed to a custom thenable are not guarded against being called more than once, or calling both fulfil and reject. A misbehaving thenable could do either.

- Each call resets `inFlight = false` and calls `drain()`. If this happens while a later request is already in flight, the serialization invariant breaks: two pumps may run at once and overwrite the shared `callback`.
- A rejection may also `finalize()` the stream after a value was already delivered.

Native promises are unaffected. Guard the callbacks with a `settled` flag.

findings.body:
In the old async generator, any exception from `stream.read()` or from reading `chunk.then` became a rejected promise, and the `finally` block cleaned up the stream. If `then` throws after `inFlight = true` is set, `inFlight` is never reset and every later `next()`/`return()` is queued forever. For thenable chunks, unwrap through a real promise, e.g. `inFlight = true; return PromisePrototypeThen(PromiseResolve(chunk), onChunkFulfilled, onChunkRejected);`. This breaks the in-order settlement the queue is meant to guarantee, for example when a consumer attaches `.then` to each request. `onChunkRejected` has the same pattern.

Suggestion: Resolve the current request first and drain afterwards, for example by deferring `drain()` with `queueMicrotask`, or by using an explicit resolve/reject pair as `pump` does.

findings.title: Slot boundary close now read off the cursor after content ran
findings.body:
The old code located the boundary's close with a structural walk from `claim.start` before `fn()` mutated or advanced anything. The trim now calls `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)` after `fn()`. Unless some inner call already cached `$fe`, that trusts `currentHydrationNode` when it rests on a close marker. `trimHydrationBoundary` documents that the cursor can be past this boundary's close, for example when a fragment claimed the close as its anchor. In that case it may rest on an enclosing `]`. `locateClaimedEnd` can then return the enclosing close and cache it as `start.$fe`, so later lookups on this open marker are wrong. The new comment in `locateClaimedEnd` describes this exact hazard. `planReuseOwnClose` for SLOT fragments (lines 241-242) has the same problem: it used to get the precomputed close and now uses the cursor-based heuristic.

Suggestion: For the slot boundary, use the structural walk, which never trusts the cursor: `trimHydrationBoundary(locateSlotEndAnchorFor(claim))`, i.e. `claim.start ? locateEndAnchor(claim.start) : null`. Use the same walk in `planReuseOwnClose` when `frag.__vf & SLOT`.

findings.title: Cached `$fe` short-circuit can return a stale or wrongly cached close
findings.body:
`locateClaimedEnd` now returns `start.$fe` unconditionally. That cache is populated by `locateEndAnchor` walks, which may run before mismatch recovery removes or replaces SSR nodes. It is also populated by any cursor-based guess this function itself stored. There is no check that the cached node is still connected or still the right kind. A detached or wrong close then propagates into `trimHydrationBoundary` and into anchor reuse.

Suggestion: Validate the cache before returning it, e.g. `if (start.$fe && start.$fe.parentNode === start.parentNode) return start.$fe`. Otherwise, only cache results that came from a structural walk.

Suggested fix: keep the guard, e.g. `const close = claim.start ? locateClaimedEnd(claim.start) : null; if (close) trimHydrationBoundary(close)`. A mismatch test where the slot has no SSR markers would confirm the behavior.

findings.title: Comma delimiter corrupts pathnames that contain commas
findings.body:
Commas are valid, unescaped characters in URL path segments (e.g. `/products/a,b` or `/tags/x,y,z`). Browsers do not percent-encode them in `location.pathname`. The client joins paths with `,`, and the server splits the decoded value back on `,`. So `/products/a,b` is reconstructed as `/products/a` and `/b`. The real path is never matched, so the needed route patches are not returned. Client-side navigation to such URLs then fails discovery and falls through to a 404/error boundary, or matches the wrong route. Under the old repeated-`p` scheme each value was carried and decoded independently, so this worked.

Suggestion: Use a delimiter that cannot appear unencoded in a pathname, or escape it. One option: on the client, `encodeURIComponent` each path before joining with `,`, then on the server split on `,` and `decodeURIComponent` each part. Alternatively, JSON-encode the array into the single param.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Old `p` query param is no longer accepted
findings.body:
The server now only recognizes `paths`. A client still running the previous bundle may hit a new server during a rolling deploy, or via a cached/custom fetcher. It sends `p=` params, `has("paths")` is false, and it gets an empty patch set with no error. Discovery then fails silently instead of falling back to a reload.

Suggestion: For a transition period, also read `url.searchParams.getAll("p")` when `paths` is absent.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Comma Path Splitting
findings.body:
The server splits the `paths` value on `,`, but commas are valid, unencoded characters in URL pathnames. `location.pathname` keeps commas as-is, for example `/tags/a,b` or `/products/1,2`. On the client, `paths.join(",")` turns `/tags/a,b` into the same string as the two paths `/tags/a` and `b`. The server then requests patches for the wrong paths, so the route is never discovered and the navigation 404s.

Previously, repeated `p` params handled these paths correctly. To fix this, encode each path before joining (for example with `encodeURIComponent`) and decode each entry after splitting. Alternatively, use a delimiter that cannot appear in a pathname.

findings.title: Fast-path check misses raw tags written without whitespace
findings.body:
`_raw_start_re` requires `\s+` between `{%` and `verbatim`/`comment`. A template that only contains `{%verbatim%}` therefore takes the plain `tag_re.split` path.

`create_token` no longer has any verbatim logic, so the verbatim body is tokenized as normal VAR/BLOCK tokens. The `verbatim` tag then renders that nodelist against an empty Context. For example, `{%verbatim%}{{ x }}{%endverbatim%}` now outputs an empty string instead of `{{ x }}`.

The old code stripped the tag content and matched `content[:9] in ("verbatim", "verbatim ")`, so this template used to work.

Suggestion: Use `\s*` in `_raw_start_re`, e.g. `r"%s\s*(?:comment|verbatim)\b"`. The precise check in `_raw_end_tag_re` already filters false positives.

Everything after the opener becomes one TEXT token, and parsing fails with an unclosed `comment`/`verbatim` tag error. Templates that rendered fine before now break.

The named-verbatim regex already uses `[^\S\n]*`, which makes the behaviour inconsistent.

Suggestion: Change `[^\S\n]+` to `[^\S\n]*` before `endcomment` and `endverbatim`. Add tests for `{%comment%}x{%endcomment%}` and `{%verbatim%}{{x}}{%endverbatim%}`.

findings.title: Sync wrapper breaks async views
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Breaks async views
findings.body:
The new `wrapper` is always a plain sync function. When `non_atomic_requests` decorates an `async def` view, `iscoroutinefunction(wrapper)` returns False. Django's handler then treats the view as sync. It calls the view in a thread and gets back an un-awaited coroutine instead of an `HttpResponse`, so the request fails ("didn't return an HttpResponse object").

This is a regression, because the previous implementation returned the original view unchanged. When `iscoroutinefunction(view)` is true, the decorator should define an `async def` wrapper that awaits the view. Alternatively, it can mark the wrapper with `markcoroutinefunction`. Adding a test with an async view would catch this.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Preserve async views when wrapping
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Sync wrapper breaks async views
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Wrapper turns async views into sync callables
findings.body:
The wrapper is a plain `def` that returns `view(...)`. When `view` is an `async def`, the wrapper is not a coroutine function. `functools.wraps` does not change that, because `iscoroutinefunction` does not follow `__wrapped__`. Django's handlers decide how to run a view with `iscoroutinefunction`. Under ASGI, an async view decorated with `@non_atomic_requests` is therefore wrapped in `sync_to_async` and returns an unawaited coroutine, which fails the response check. Under WSGI the view also returns a coroutine instead of a response. Before this change the decorator only set an attribute and left the view untouched, so async views worked. Any existing async view using this decorator now breaks.

Suggestion: Pick the wrapper type from the view. For an async view, define `async def wrapper(*args, **kwargs): return await view(*args, **kwargs)`. Otherwise use the sync wrapper. Alternatively, copy the view and set the attribute without wrapping, for example with `types.FunctionType` or `functools.partial` plus `markcoroutinefunction`. Add a test for an async view.

findings.title: Hard-coded sort_keys collides with user-supplied option
findings.body:
Extra keyword arguments given to `serializers.serialize('yaml', ..., sort_keys=True)` are stored in `self.options` and splatted into `yaml.dump`. The call now also passes `sort_keys=False` explicitly. If a caller provides `sort_keys`, Python raises `TypeError: dump() got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'`. Before this change the option was accepted (and effectively overridden by the dict representer), so this is a regression that crashes serialization for such callers. It also makes the default impossible to override.

Suggestion: self.options.setdefault("allow_unicode", True)
self.options.setdefault("sort_keys", False)
yaml.dump(self.objects, self.stream, Dumper=DjangoSafeDumper, **self.options)

findings.body:
`sort_keys=False` is passed explicitly, and `**self.options` is also passed. If a caller passes `sort_keys` to the serializer, the call raises `TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'`. Example: `serializers.serialize("yaml", qs, sort_keys=True)`.

Before this change, that option was forwarded to `yaml.dump` without error. It had no effect because of the dict representer, but it did not crash.

Use `self.options.setdefault("sort_keys", False)`, as is already done for `allow_unicode`. This keeps the default and also lets callers override it.

findings.title: Plain ndarray `out=` drops subclass type of delta
findings.body:
Before this change, `np.subtract(stop, start, ...)` let subclasses of the inputs flow through `__array_wrap__`/`__array_ufunc__`. For example, a MaskedArray delta kept its mask. Now the array path always writes into `np.zeros(...)`, which is a base ndarray. Subclass information is lost, and later arithmetic such as `y = y * delta` produces a different type or mask than before. This changes behaviour for subclasses that rely on linspace's generic path without overriding `__array_function__`.

Suggestion: Build the zero output with the input's array type, e.g. `out = np.zeros_like(np.broadcast_arrays(stop, start)[0], dtype=type(dt))`. Alternatively, compute `delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt))` inside `np.errstate(invalid='ignore')` only where needed, then apply `delta = np.where(equal, 0, delta)`, which preserves subclass dispatch.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Avoid unconditional plain-array output allocation
findings.body:
The array branch always writes into a freshly allocated plain `np.zeros` buffer, even when no endpoints are equal. This silently drops array subclasses and their extra state, such as masks or units, that the original `np.subtract(stop, start, ...)` preserved, so `linspace` can behave differently for subclass inputs. Use the original subtraction unless some elements are actually equal, and use the `where=` path only in that case.

Improved code:
equal = start == stop
if equal.ndim == 0:
    delta = dt.type(0) if equal else np.subtract(
        stop, start, dtype=type(dt))
elif not equal.any():
    delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt))
else:
    delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt), where=~equal,
                        out=np.zeros(equal.shape, dtype=type(dt)))

findings.title: Zero-filled `out` buffer and scalar `dt.type(0)` drop subclass information from `delta`
findings.body:
Before, `delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=...)` ran on the converted inputs, so ndarray subclasses (such as unit-carrying or masked arrays) could propagate their type through `__array_wrap__`/`__array_ufunc__`. Now the 0-d equal case returns a bare numpy scalar and the array case writes into a plain `np.zeros` ndarray. `delta`, `step` and hence `y` can then lose the subclass, units or mask. The code before this change was written so the result class could be driven by `delta`, and the original comment says as much. The behaviour change is silent: it affects every `linspace` call with subclass inputs, not only the equal-infinity case. Also, `equal = start == stop` runs an extra comparison on every call. The comparison can return a non-ndarray or non-bool object for exotic subclasses, which would break `.ndim` or `~equal`.

Suggestion: Keep the original `np.subtract` for the general path and only patch the equal-endpoint elements. For example, compute `delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt), where=~equal, out=...)` with `out` allocated by `np.empty_like`/`np.zeros_like` of a result that preserves the subclass, or use `with np.errstate(invalid='ignore'): delta = ...; delta = np.where(equal, 0, delta)` limited to the `inf - inf` case.

findings.title: Backslash-leading replacement bypasses the collapse
findings.body:
`newPath` is normalized here, but further down `RedirectRule` prepends '/' when `newPath[0] != '/'`. A replacement such as `$1`, capturing `\evil.com`, is not collapsed because it lacks a leading '/'. It later becomes `/\evil.com` and is emitted in the Location header, which is still a scheme-relative open redirect.

Suggestion: Apply `CollapseLeadingSlashes` after the leading-'/' prefix is added, or make the normalizer treat a leading '\' the same as '/'.

findings.title: Same ordering gap, plus a silent behavior change for internal rewrites
findings.body:
As in the redirect paths, a pattern starting with '\' is not collapsed and is later prefixed with '/', producing `/\host`. This call also changes `Request.Path` for every internal rewrite whose target begins with `//`. Apps that relied on preserving those segments will break even though no Location header is involved.

Suggestion: Normalize after the '/' prefix is applied, and document the behavior change (or limit it to redirect actions).

findings.title: Normalizer ignores inputs that begin with '\'

The guard returns early unless `url[0] == '/'`. Inputs like `\\evil.com` or `\/evil.com` are returned unchanged, even though callers then turn them into scheme-relative URLs. The helper is only safe if every caller invokes it after ensuring a leading '/', and none of them currently do.

Suggestion: Accept either '/' or '\' at index 0, collapse the whole leading run of slashes and backslashes, and return a string with a single leading '/'.

Suggestion: Unit-test `UrlNormalizer` and the rule/action classes directly with backslash inputs, or set the request path via `TestServer.SendAsync` so it is not normalized.

findings.title: Normalization bypass
findings.body:
`CollapseLeadingSlashes` runs before the code that prepends `/` to relative patterns, and it only acts when the string already starts with `/`. A pattern that starts with a backslash skips normalization, then gets `/` prepended, which recreates the scheme-relative shape.

Example: the IIS rule `url="{R:1}"` with a capture of `\example.com` (or `\\example.com`) becomes `/\example.com`. Browsers treat that as `//example.com`, so the open redirect still works. The same applies to Apache rules like `RewriteRule /legacy/(.*) $1 [R=302]`.

Fix: normalize after the leading `/` is prepended, or make the helper also collapse a leading run that begins with `\`. Add test cases where the target has no leading `/` and the capture starts with `\`.

findings.title: End-anchor heuristic uses stale/zero Bounds
findings.body:
The new check compares the viewport end with `Bounds.Width/Height`. Those bounds come from the previous arrange, not from the current extent estimate. Three cases go wrong:

- **Before the first arrange:** Bounds is 0, so any non-negative viewport end passes. The only guard is `!_hasReachedEnd`, so the first realization can anchor on the last item at `viewportEnd - estimate` instead of index 0.
- **After the items change:** after an add, remove or reset, the old Bounds no longer match the content, yet the panel can still be forced to the end.
- **Panel stretched to the viewport:** when the panel is stretched to the viewport size (content smaller than the viewport), viewportEnd == Bounds whenever `_hasReachedEnd` happens to be false. The layout is then built backwards from the last item and the first items can be pushed to negative positions.

Each case mis-positions realized items or causes an unexpected jump to the end.

Suggestion: Compare against the panel's own estimated extent for the current item count, such as the last measured extent or `EstimateElementSizeU() * itemCount` combined with realized sizes. Also require that a previous measure/arrange has actually happened, for example a valid `_lastEstimatedElementSizeU` or `Bounds` that is not empty.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: End-of-viewport condition duplicated across methods
findings.body:
The `viewportEnd >= Bounds` check together with `!_hasReachedEnd` is computed independently in the anchor estimation and again in RealizeElements. `anchorAtEnd` is only correct if both copies stay in sync and `_hasReachedEnd` has not changed between them. Any future change to one copy will silently desynchronize the anchor index from the anchor position correction.

Suggestion: Compute the 'anchor at end' decision once, for example as a flag returned with the viewport/anchor tuple, and reuse it in RealizeElements.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Stale Bounds check

The new "anchor at end" shortcut compares the current viewport end with `Bounds.Width`/`Bounds.Height`. During measure, `Bounds` still holds the previous arrange size, so the panel compares against the old extent.

Example scenario:
- The items source is replaced or grows a lot (say 100 → 1000 items) while the viewport sits at the old end.
- `_hasReachedEnd` is false at that point.
- `viewportEnd >= oldBounds` passes, so the anchor jumps to `itemCount - 1`.
- The scroll position snaps to the end of the new list instead of keeping the current offset.

The same stale comparison feeds `anchorAtEnd` in `RealizeElements`.

Uncertain: whether `_hasReachedEnd` is always still true in these reset or growth paths. If it is, the shortcut is skipped.

Possible fix: base the condition on the estimated or known extent for the current item count rather than the last arranged `Bounds`.

The anchor then becomes the last item at `viewportEnd - estimatedSize`, and the list starts realised from the end instead of the start. The same stale comparison can fire after the panel is resized, when items or the viewport change, or when all items fit and `_hasReachedEnd` hasn't been set yet. Offset 0 is then not honoured and the layout jumps.

Suggestion: Detect the end from the scroll offset and estimated extent rather than `Bounds`. For example, compare `viewportEnd` to the extent computed from the realised elements, or have ScrollViewer/ScrollToEnd set an explicit 'scroll to end' flag that this code consumes. At minimum, skip the shortcut when `Bounds` is empty or the viewport offset is 0.

findings.title: Duplicated end-detection logic and unclamped anchor position
findings.body:
The 'at end' condition is recomputed here, separately from the anchor selection code. The two copies depend on `_hasReachedEnd` and `Bounds` and can drift apart. When they disagree, for example when the anchor was chosen by the normal path and happens to be the last index, `u` is overwritten with `viewportEnd - sizeU`. The overwritten value can be negative when the last item is taller than the viewport, or when the content is shorter than the viewport. That places the realised elements at a negative start position.

Suggestion: Compute the 'anchor at end' decision once, store it in a field or in the returned anchor tuple, and clamp `u` (for example `Math.Max(0, ...)`), or only apply it when the anchor was chosen by the end-detection path.

findings.title: Pointer popups lose edge-constraint adjustment after the first arrange
findings.body:
After the first arrange sets `_hasInitialPosition`, every later size change for a Pointer-placed popup skips `UpdatePosition()`. That method also applies the anchor and gravity constraint adjustment: flipping and sliding the popup so it stays on screen.

This fails in two ways:
- If the first arrange happens before the content reaches its final size (lazy templates, async content, items loading), the popup keeps a position computed for the wrong size.
- If the popup later grows near a screen edge, it extends off-screen instead of being flipped or clamped.

This is a regression for context menus opened near the bottom or right edge.

Suggestion: Instead of skipping `UpdatePosition` entirely, keep the original pointer anchor point fixed and still run the constraint logic. Alternatively, only suppress repositioning when the new bounds still fit within the screen's working area.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Flag is never reset when the position request changes
findings.body:
`_hasInitialPosition` is cleared only in `Dispose`. If `ConfigurePosition` installs a new request on the same root (new pointer location, or a placement change) and relies on the next arrange to apply it, the Pointer-placement short-circuit suppresses that repositioning. The flag is also set for non-Pointer placements, so if the placement later switches to Pointer, the very first arrange for that placement is suppressed too.

Suggestion: Reset `_hasInitialPosition = false` wherever `_popupPositionRequest` is assigned (`ConfigurePosition`). Only set it to true when the placement is Pointer.

findings.title: DeleteExpression compiled with CommandSource.ExecuteUpdate
findings.body:
The `DeleteExpression` branch passes `CommandSource.ExecuteUpdate` to `GenerateNonQueryShaper`. Previously, `NonQueryExpression(DeleteExpression)` used `CommandSource.ExecuteDelete`. Every ExecuteDelete call now reports itself as ExecuteUpdate to command interceptors, diagnostics/logging events and the concurrency/thread-safety detector. Interceptors or telemetry that branch on `CommandSource.ExecuteDelete` will stop seeing deletes, and update-specific handling will run for deletes instead.

Suggestion: DeleteExpression deleteExpression => GenerateNonQueryShaper(deleteExpression.ApplyTags(_tags), CommandSource.ExecuteDelete),

findings.title: Removed protected virtual VisitNonQuery extensibility point

The public `NonQueryExpression` type and the protected virtual `VisitNonQuery` hook are deleted outright, without obsoletion. Third-party relational providers that override `VisitNonQuery` or construct/match `NonQueryExpression` will fail to compile. They also lose a clean hook to customize non-query execution: they must now override `VisitExtension` and re-implement the update/delete dispatch, including tag application and command-source selection.

Suggestion: Keep a `protected virtual Expression VisitNonQuery(Expression nonQueryExpression, CommandSource commandSource)` (or similar) hook that `VisitExtension` delegates to, so providers retain an override point; document the breaking change.

findings.title: Panic on readiness without exit status
findings.body:
After `poll_read_ready` reports ready, the code calls `try_wait()` and `expect`s `Some`. Readiness from the reactor can be spurious or stale, for example after a `reregister` or an error/HUP event delivered by mio. In that case `try_wait()` returns `Ok(None)` and the future panics inside the user's `.await`. The signal-based reaper tolerates this by re-polling.

Suggestion: If `try_wait()` returns `None`, clear the readiness (use the guard's `clear_readiness`, or keep the `ReadyEvent` and call `registration.clear_readiness(ev)`) and return `Poll::Pending` instead of panicking.

Suggestion: Probe support directly instead, e.g. by checking whether `Pidfd::open(std::process::id())` returns `Some`. If you keep the version check, trim the string and split on `|c: char| !c.is_ascii_digit()`.

findings.title: EINVAL on kernels 5.3-5.9 is not cached
findings.body:
`PIDFD_NONBLOCK` is only supported since Linux 5.10. On 5.3-5.9, `pidfd_open` returns EINVAL, not ENOSYS. Because only ENOSYS sets `NO_PIDFD_SUPPORT`, every spawn on those kernels pays a failing syscall before falling back to the signal reaper.

Suggestion: Also set `NO_PIDFD_SUPPORT` when errno is `EINVAL`. Alternatively, open without `PIDFD_NONBLOCK`, since the fd is only polled and never read.

findings.title: Dropped pidfd children may never be reaped because no SIGCHLD listener exists
findings.body:
When a PidfdReaper is dropped before the child exits, the child is pushed to the global orphan queue. That queue is only drained from the signal-based path (the SIGCHLD listener in `Reaper`) or on later spawns. In the pidfd path no `signal(SignalKind::child())` is created, so nothing may ever drive `reap_orphans`. Those children can stay zombies indefinitely, especially in programs that only use pidfd-based children. This is a behavioural regression from the signal-based reaper, which always had a signal stream registered.

Suggestion: Register or keep a SIGCHLD listener (or otherwise trigger orphan reaping) when pushing to the orphan queue. Alternatively, drain the queue from a pidfd-based mechanism.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Child is leaked as a zombie when PollEvented registration fails
findings.body:
In the `Err((Some(err), _child))` arm the std child is dropped without being waited on or pushed to the orphan queue. If the process later exits it stays a zombie. Registration errors (e.g. epoll limits) are plausible under resource pressure. Dropping `std::process::Child` neither kills nor reaps it.

Suggestion: Before returning the error, push `_child` to the `GlobalOrphanQueue` (or kill and wait it) so it is reaped.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: expect() on try_wait panics instead of handling a not-yet-reapable child
findings.body:
The code assumes that pidfd readiness implies `try_wait()` returns `Some`. If it returns `None` (for example, readiness from an unexpected event, or a nonstandard wait state), the poll panics inside the runtime instead of returning an error or re-polling. A library should not panic on a kernel/ABI assumption.

Suggestion: If `try_wait()` returns `Ok(None)`, clear readiness and return `Poll::Pending` (waking itself), or return an `io::Error`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Possible Bug
findings.body: `Pidfd::open` treats every `pidfd_open` failure as "no pidfd support" and returns `None`, and `PidfdReaper::new` then returns `Err((None, child))`, so the caller silently falls back to the signal reaper. That fallback is reasonable for ENOSYS, but `PIDFD_NONBLOCK` is only accepted by kernels 5.10+. On kernels 5.3-5.9, `pidfd_open` fails with EINVAL on every call. The `NO_PIDFD_SUPPORT` cache is only set for ENOSYS, so each spawn repeats a failing syscall. This is only a performance cost. The cache could also cover EINVAL.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Panic Risk
findings.body: `poll` calls `.expect("pidfd is ready to read, the process should have exited")` on the result of `try_wait()`. A pidfd becomes readable when the process exits, so this is normally true. However, `Child` is publicly exposed and `try_wait`/`kill` go through `std_child()`. If a user calls `try_wait()` and reaps the child before the future is polled, the next `try_wait` in `poll` may return an error (ECHILD) or `Ok(None)`, and the `expect` panics. The semantics of the std `Child` also make `Ok(None)` possible under other conditions (e.g. spurious readiness). Returning an error or re-polling is safer than panicking.

findings.title: Inverted check disables semantic diagnostics after build data/proc-macros load
findings.body:
The comment says diagnostics should be fetched only after build data and proc-macros have finished loading once. The code instead requires `last_op_result().is_none()`, which is only true while the op has never completed.

Build scripts and proc-macros are enabled by default. Once their first run finishes, `last_op_result()` becomes `Some` and `fetch_semantic` stays false for the rest of the session. Semantic diagnostics then silently stop working for every user with default settings.

During the brief window before any build has started, the check passes (`None` and not in progress). So diagnostics are computed exactly when the comment says they should not be.

Suggestion: let fetch_semantic = self.vfs_done
    && self.fetch_workspaces_queue.last_op_result().is_some()
    && (!self.config.run_build_scripts(None)
        || (self.fetch_build_data_queue.last_op_result().is_some()
            && !self.fetch_build_data_queue.op_in_progress()))
    && (!self.config.expand_proc_macros()
        || (self.fetch_proc_macros_queue.last_op_result().is_some()
            && !self.fetch_proc_macros_queue.op_in_progress()));
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Diagnostics vanish on every rebuild, not just the initial load
findings.body:
The `!op_in_progress()` checks also apply after the first successful load. Every subsequent build-script or proc-macro rerun (for example after editing Cargo.toml or build.rs) stops semantic diagnostics from being fetched until the rerun finishes. This contradicts the stated intent of "finished ... once", and diagnostics may flicker or disappear during long rebuilds.

Suggestion: Gate only on `last_op_result().is_some()`, which means the op has completed at least once, and drop the `op_in_progress()` conditions.

findings.title: Inverted Condition
findings.body:

With the default config, where build scripts and proc-macro expansion are enabled:
- Before the first build-data or proc-macro load finishes, `fetch_semantic` is true. This is the case the PR is meant to prevent.
- Once each load has completed and `last_op_result()` becomes `Some`, `fetch_semantic` stays false. Semantic diagnostics are then permanently disabled for the session.

Both checks should be `last_op_result().is_some() && !op_in_progress()`.

findings.title: Retry decision relies on fragile error-message substring matching
findings.body:
`isResourceQuotaConflict` decides retryability by searching the formatted error string for two hard-coded phrases. These phrases come from the apiserver's generic `NewConflict` message format and the `resourcequotas` resource name. They are not part of a stable API.

The check can silently stop matching if any of these change:
- the apiserver wording or localization;
- a proxy or webhook that rewrites the message;
- an upstream change to the conflict text.

If that happens, transient quota conflicts fail again and no test against a real server would notice. The structured `StatusError` details already carry the conflicting resource, which is a sturdier signal.

Suggestion: Inspect structured details instead of the message, e.g.
```go
var se *apierrors.StatusError
if errors.As(err, &se) && se.ErrStatus.Details != nil && se.ErrStatus.Details.Kind == "resourcequotas" {
    return true
}
```
Keep the substring check only as a fallback.

findings.title: DefaultRetry backoff is too short to resolve quota contention
findings.body:
`retry.DefaultRetry` is 5 steps, 10ms base delay and factor 1.0, so all retries finish within roughly 40-50ms. Quota conflicts happen when many objects are created in the same namespace concurrently, and `ResourceQuota` is not fully retried server-side. That window may be too short under real contention. In that case the user still gets the conflict error, only after five wasted PATCH calls. Each failed attempt also logs the same debug error line.

Suggestion: Use a dedicated `wait.Backoff` with exponential growth (for example Duration 100ms, Factor 2, Steps 5, Jitter 0.1).
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Retry decision depends on matching server error message text
findings.body:
`isResourceQuotaConflict` identifies the quota case by substring-matching the error message ("Operation cannot be fulfilled on resourcequotas" and "the object has been modified"). These strings are not an API contract. A change to the apiserver wording, or to how `patchResourceServerSide` wraps the error, silently disables the retry, and nothing flags it. The check also matches the message of any wrapped error. The `StatusError` details are more reliable: `Details.Kind` is "resourcequotas" for this error, and `Details.Group` and `Details.Name` are also available.

Suggestion: Use `var se apierrors.APIStatus; if errors.As(err, &se) { d := se.Status().Details; return d != nil && d.Kind == "resourcequotas" }` and keep the message check only as a fallback.
findings.label: nit

The message match could stay as a fallback. This is a robustness concern rather than a confirmed bug, because the current message format is stable today.

findings.title: Check other users of the Control D ranges for consistency
findings.body:
The range-based upgrade was removed only from `DoHEndpointFromIP`. `controlDv6RangeA`/`controlDv6RangeB` (and `controlDBase`) are still defined in this package. If `IPIsDoHOnlyServer` or similar helpers still match the full /48, they would still report the ID-encoded addresses as DoH-only. That contradicts the new behaviour, where those addresses are plain port-53 resolvers and `DoHEndpointFromIP` returns `ok=false`. Callers that trust the DoH-only classification (e.g. by routing such resolvers through the forwarder or skipping plain-UDP use) could then mishandle these resolvers. If the ranges are no longer referenced at all, they are dead code.

Suggestion: Update `IPIsDoHOnlyServer` (and any other user of `controlDv6RangeA`/`B`) so it no longer treats the Control D /48 as DoH-only, or delete the ranges if they are now unused. Add a test asserting `IPIsDoHOnlyServer(2606:1a40:0:6:7b5b:5949:35ad:0) == false`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Fallback is ignored when the global symbol already exists
findings.body:
The global dispatcher property is often installed before globalThis is frozen, either by undici's own module init or by Node's bundled fetch. After the freeze, defineProperty with a new value throws TypeError, so the agent is written to `fallbackDispatcher`. But `getGlobalDispatcher` returns `globalThis[globalDispatcher] ?? fallbackDispatcher`, and the stale global value is non-nullish. The newly set agent is therefore never returned. setGlobalDispatcher appears to succeed but has no effect, and nothing reports the failure.

Suggestion: Track explicitly whether the fallback is active, e.g. `let useFallback = false`, set it to true in the catch, and in getGlobalDispatcher do `return useFallback ? fallbackDispatcher : globalThis[globalDispatcher]`. Alternatively, warn or throw when the global cannot be updated.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Fallback path skips the legacy dispatcher and cross-copy sharing
findings.body:
When the fallback is used, the function returns before updating `legacyGlobalDispatcher`. Legacy (v1) consumers that read that symbol keep the old dispatcher or get undefined. The fallback is also module-local, so other undici copies and Node's built-in fetch, which read the global symbol, never see the dispatcher that was set. The global-symbol design exists precisely to share the dispatcher across copies.

Suggestion: Document that the frozen-global fallback is per-module-instance. Also keep a fallback legacy wrapper, so code paths that resolve the legacy dispatcher through this module stay consistent.

The error is swallowed. The primary symbol then points to the new agent while the legacy symbol still points to the old one, and nothing indicates the mismatch.

findings.title: Stale dispatcher returned
findings.body:
Updates are silently lost if `globalThis` is frozen after the global dispatcher symbol already exists.

This happens in the common case: undici, or Node's bundled fetch, sets the dispatcher first, and the app calls `Object.freeze(globalThis)` later. Freezing makes the existing property non-writable, so a later `setGlobalDispatcher(newAgent)` fails in `defineProperty`. The `TypeError` is caught and `newAgent` goes into `fallbackDispatcher`.

However, `getGlobalDispatcher` returns `globalThis[globalDispatcher] ?? fallbackDispatcher`. The global property is still the old agent, so the fallback is never read. The call appears to succeed but has no effect, and requests keep using the old agent.

Fix options:
- Have `getGlobalDispatcher` prefer `fallbackDispatcher` once it is set.
- Or clear `fallbackDispatcher` on a successful define and check it first.

findings.title: Fallback is shadowed by a previously defined global dispatcher
findings.body:
If undici loaded normally (the module-load call defines the symbol on globalThis) and globalThis is frozen afterwards, the symbol property becomes non-writable. A later setGlobalDispatcher() then makes defineProperty throw TypeError, which is caught and the agent goes into fallbackDispatcher. getGlobalDispatcher() reads `globalThis[globalDispatcher] ?? fallbackDispatcher`. The old value is still defined, so it wins and the new dispatcher is silently ignored. The call appears to succeed but has no effect. findings.title: Swallowed cache delete leaves invalidated session readable
findings.body:
The cached_db backend serves `load()` from the cache first and only falls back to the DB on a miss. Before this change, a failed cache delete raised an error, so a logout or `flush()` visibly failed.

Now the DB row is deleted, the cache delete error is only logged, and the old session data, including the auth user id, stays in the cache until it expires. Anyone holding the old session cookie (for example a stolen or fixated key) can keep using the authenticated session after the user logs out.

This is worse than the existing write-failure handling. A failed write leaves stale data, but a failed delete leaves a session the user explicitly ended still usable.

Suggestion: When the cache delete fails, make sure the stale cache entry cannot be trusted. Options:
- Retry the delete, or overwrite the entry with a short-TTL tombstone that `load()` treats as a miss.
- Have `load()` check the DB when the cached entry might be stale.
- At minimum, re-raise when called from `flush()`/logout, so session invalidation never fails silently. The docs should also call out that the stale entry remains.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Silent stale session
findings.body: `cached_db` reads from the cache before the database. If the cache delete fails, the DB row is gone but the cached session data stays valid until the cache entry expires. Before this change, the exception made `delete()` and `flush()` (used by `logout()`) fail visibly. Now logout looks successful while a copy of the session cookie can still authenticate until cache expiry. Swallowing errors is fine for `save()`, but for `delete()` it is a security trade-off. Consider documenting this explicitly, or retrying or invalidating the entry another way (e.g. setting a short-lived tombstone).

The stale cache entry also existed before this PR; the new part is that the failure is no longer surfaced to the caller.

findings.title: Regression test does not verify the deferred recompute happened
findings.body:
The test only checks that `IsOpen` is true and that the button's own `IsVisible` is false. It does not check:
- that the visibility change actually happened during popup opening (the button may already be parented earlier, e.g. when added to the collection or on `CreateWindow`);

findings.title: Deferred update flag is left set if opening the popup throws
findings.body:
ApplyDeferredDynamicOverflowUpdate sits after the try/finally. If `_overflowPopup.IsOpen = true` throws, the finally clears `_isOpeningOverflowPopup` but the deferral is never applied or cleared. The overflow state therefore stays stale until some later trigger. `_hasDeferredDynamicOverflowUpdate` also stays true. findings.title: Race Condition
findings.body:
`Parallel.ForEach` updates the static `Dictionary` `TotalsByCustomer` from multiple threads with a read-modify-write. `Dictionary` is not thread-safe, so concurrent rows can lose updates, corrupt the dictionary, or throw. Any CSV large enough to run rows in parallel can trigger this, especially when several rows share a customer.

Related problems in the same method:
- `async void` means callers cannot await completion. Exceptions from a missing file, malformed rows (`cols[3]` out of range, `decimal.Parse`), or HTTP failures in `ToUsd` go unobserved or crash the process.
- `StreamReader` is never disposed, so the file handle leaks.
- Each parallel row makes a blocking HTTP call through `RateService.ToUsd`. It creates a new `HttpClient` per call and blocks with `.Result`, which risks socket exhaustion and thread-pool starvation.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Off-by-one
findings.body:
The loop condition `i <= start + size` returns `size + 1` items whenever enough items exist. For example, `Window(items, 0, 10)` returns 11 elements. Use `i < start + size`.

A negative `start` also throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` from the indexer. A negative `size` throws from the `List` constructor. Unlike `Page`, neither argument is validated.

notes: SQL injection: In `OrdersController.CountMatching`, `customerPrefix` is concatenated directly into the SQL text. An input like `x' OR 1=1; DROP TABLE orders; --` lets an attacker run arbitrary SQL. Insecure password reset token: `PasswordHasher.ResetToken` computes MD5 of `email + yyyyMMdd`, with no secret or randomness. Anyone who knows a user's email can compute that day's valid token and reset the password, which allows account takeover. Use a cryptographically random token (`RandomNumberGenerator`) stored server-side with an expiry and single use, or an HMAC with a server secret.

findings.title: Overflow Bypasses Cap
findings.body: `1 << attempt` overflows for large attempt counts, so the `d > 30` cap never applies. On 64-bit platforms, `attempt` = 63 yields a negative value and `attempt` >= 64 yields 0. A long-running retry loop that keeps incrementing `attempt` would then wait zero or a negative duration and spin without backoff. A negative `attempt` panics at runtime. Clamp `attempt` before shifting, for example by returning 30 when `attempt >= 5` and treating `attempt < 0` as 0.

The callers are not in this diff, so verify that every call site was updated for the new unit, or rename the function or return a `time.Duration` so the change can't be missed.

findings.title: Guard against missing user lookup
findings.body:
A lookup like `FindUser` typically returns nil when the user is missing, such as when the owner has been deleted or the ID is invalid. Dereferencing `u` without a check will then panic. Guard against nil before accessing `Email`.

Improved code:
u := s.FindUser(ownerID)
	if u == nil {
		return ""
	}
	return u.Email
findings.label: defect:nilderef

findings.title: Handle missing administrator safely
findings.body:
`s.Admin()` may return nil if no administrator is configured, and dereferencing it would panic while rendering the report footer. Check the result before reading `Email`.

Improved code:
a := s.Admin()
	if a == nil {
		return ""
	}
	return a.Email

findings.title: Shift overflow / panic
findings.body: `1 << attempt` is computed before the cap is applied. For `attempt` of 63, the result is `math.MinInt64`, which is negative and passes the `d > 30` check, so a negative delay is returned. For `attempt` >= 64 the result is 0, so there is no backoff at all. A negative `attempt` panics at runtime. A long-running retry loop would hit these cases and either spin with no delay or pass a negative duration to a sleep. Clamp `attempt` (for example, return 30 once `attempt >= 5`, and treat negatives as 0) before shifting.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Unit change
findings.body: The exported `Delay` changed from returning milliseconds (`100 << attempt`) to seconds (`1 << attempt`, capped at 30). Any caller still treating the value as milliseconds would now wait about 1000x less. I could not see the callers in this diff, so this needs verification, and the change is not mentioned in the PR description.

findings.title: Wrong Path/Types
findings.body:
Image/CSV diff regresses for renamed and copied files. The right-side blob is fetched from `rightCommit` using `diffFile.OldName` instead of `diffFile.Name`. That bug existed before, but these blobs now also drive image detection, `RightBlob`/`RightBlobSize`/`RightBlobMimeType` and the CSV diff.

Both branches are also gated on `Type` being `Add`, `Del` or `Change`. For `DiffFileRename` and `DiffFileCopy`, no blob is loaded at all. So `IsBlobTypeImage` is false and `LeftBlob`/`RightBlob` are nil.

Result:
- A renamed or copied image no longer shows the image diff.
- A renamed or copied CSV is diffed against nil blobs.

The old template looked up `$.BeforeCommit`/`$file.OldName` and `$.HeadCommit`/`$file.Name` regardless of type. Fix: use `diffFile.Name` for the right side, and include rename/copy types when loading blobs for render info.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Performance Regression
findings.body:
Every binary file in a diff is now streamed in full, on both sides, during each render. Previously `IsBin` files returned early, and content sniffing only read `SniffContentSize` bytes.

`getCommitFileBlobAndLimitedContent` calls `GetBlobLineCount`, which reads the entire blob just to count lines and bytes. The limit only caps what is buffered, not what is read. A PR or commit touching large binaries (e.g. archives, videos of hundreds of MB) will read all of that data on every diff page load.

For binaries, read only the sniff prefix and get the size from `blob.Size`, or by another cheap means.

findings.title: Use new file name for right blob

The right side (after commit) is looked up by `diffFile.OldName`. For renamed files this returns the wrong blob or none, which breaks `RightBlob`, its size, MIME type, image/CSV detection and highlighting. The old template correctly used `$file.Name` for the head commit, so use `diffFile.Name` here.

Improved code:
if (diffFile.Type == DiffFileAdd || diffFile.Type == DiffFileChange) && rightCommit != nil {
		c := getCommitFileBlobAndLimitedContent(ctx, gitRepo, rightCommit, diffFile.Name, contentLimit)

findings.title: Propagate line counts to render detail
findings.body:
`prepareDiffRenderDetail` stores the line counts only in the local variables `leftLineCount` and `rightLineCount`. It never copies them into `ret.leftLineCount` and `ret.rightLineCount`. As a result, `addTailSection` builds the tail section with `LeftIdx`/`RightIdx` set to 0, which breaks expanding the remaining lines. Assign the counts to `ret` before returning.

Improved code:
if leftLineCount <= lastLine.LeftIdx || rightLineCount <= lastLine.RightIdx {
		return ret
	}
	ret.needTailSection = true
	ret.leftLineCount, ret.rightLineCount = leftLineCount, rightLineCount
	return ret

findings.title: Renamed images/CSVs lose blobs
findings.body: `LeftBlob`/`RightBlob` are only loaded when `Type` is Add, Del or Change. The old templates fetched both blobs by path for every file, including renamed ones. A renamed (and possibly modified) image now gets empty `LeftBlobMimeType`/`RightBlobMimeType`, so `IsBlobTypeImage` is false and the image diff is no longer rendered. A renamed CSV gets nil blobs passed to `CreateCsvDiff`. In addition, the right blob is looked up with `diffFile.OldName` instead of `diffFile.Name`, which is wrong whenever the names differ. Load the left blob by `OldName` and the right blob by `Name`, and cover rename types too.

findings.body: For binary files the content limit is `SniffContentSize`. `getCommitFileBlobAndLimitedContent` still calls `GetBlobLineCount`, which streams the entire blob through `DataAsync` and counts newlines. The old code skipped binary files entirely. Diffs containing large binaries (archives, videos, large images) now read each full blob from git on both sides just to get the size, which can slow or time out the diff page. For binary files, get the size via a cheaper path and read only the sniff prefix.

findings.title: Errors Discarded
findings.body: `err = errors.Join(srvHalfCloser.CloseRead())` and `err = errors.Join(srvHalfCloser.CloseWrite())` do not include the existing `err`. This overwrites the `io.Copy` error and the client half-close error. Whenever `srv` is a HalfCloser, which is the normal case, copy failures such as "from backend to client" are lost, and `handleTCP` usually returns nil. Use `errors.Join(err, ...)` instead, as in the client branch.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Possible Hang
findings.body:
`handleTCP` now waits for both copy goroutines before returning, so the deferred `srv.Close()` runs only after both finish. When one direction ends, only a half-close is propagated. The other `io.Copy` stays blocked until that peer closes its side.

If either conn is not a `nettype.HalfCloser`, nothing unblocks the second copy. This happens with a custom `Server.Dialer` returning a non-TCP conn, or with `connWithOneByte` wrapping a non-TCP conn, where the methods are silent no-ops. Previously the first finishing direction tore down both sides. Now the goroutines and connections can leak indefinitely, for example after a backend reset or full close while the client keeps its socket open.

Fall back to fully closing both conns when half-close is unsupported, or after an error in either direction.

Now `handleTCP` waits for both goroutines. If one direction fails (for example a reset, or a write error to a dead peer), the other direction's `io.Copy` stays blocked on a connection that nothing closes, so the SOCKS handler and its goroutines can hang until the peer closes. On the success path, half-close handles the shutdown. On the error path, the connections should be fully closed so the other copy unblocks.

In `handleTCP`, `CloseRead` is called from the backend-to-client goroutine while `Read` runs in the client-to-backend goroutine's `io.Copy`, so this is a data race and will be flagged by `-race`. Also, `readClosed` makes `Read` return `net.ErrClosed`, which `io.Copy` reports as an error even though a half-close is expected. It only matters when `CloseRead` is called while a `Read` is in progress.
