findings.body:
This callback returns `nil` error on a retryable status, so the pacer retries and overwrites `res`. The previous response body is never closed.

Retries now cover 500/502/503/504/509 instead of only 429. A run of transient server errors during downloads can therefore leak one body and connection per attempt.

Close or drain `res.Body` before returning `true`.

findings.title: Response body leak on retry
findings.body: In the `Open` download paths, a retryable status such as 502 or 503 returns `true, nil` without closing `res.Body` (or `downloadRes.Body`). Each retry overwrites the response, so the earlier body and its connection are leaked. Retries now fire for 500/502/503/504/509 as well as 429, so this is far more likely to happen. If retries are exhausted, the pacer returns a nil error, and the caller then treats the 5xx response as a successful download. Close the body before returning retry=true, and return an error carrying the status so exhausted retries fail.

findings.body:
`s.f.srv.Call` returns a non-error response for HTTP 4xx/5xx statuses only if the rest client treats them as errors. If `opts.ContentLength` is not set, a fresh `bytes.NewReader` body may be sent chunked, which breaks presigned S3 PUT uploads. findings.title: Hidden host capabilities
findings.body:
`hostWrapper` embeds `component.Host` as an interface, so only `GetExtensions` (plus the explicitly added `Report`/`RegisterZPages`) is promoted. Any other optional capability on the real service host is lost to extensions.

Extensions find these capabilities with type assertions, so they would now fail. Examples include `GetFactory` (`hostcapabilities.ComponentFactoryProvider`) and `GetModuleInfos` (`hostcapabilities.ModuleInfo`). Extensions that use them, such as an OpAMP-style extension reporting module info, would silently lose that functionality.

Fix: forward these interfaces too, the same way `RegisterZPages` is forwarded. Alternatively, build the wrapper dynamically so it preserves the underlying host's interfaces. Add tests asserting those capabilities still pass through.

findings.title: Datapath/userspace mismatch
findings.body:
The new ID-0 fallback lookup runs only when both the specific and aggregate lookups miss. It also has no counterpart in the Go `mapState.lookup`, which only considers the specific ID and `aggregateFor(key.Identity)`.

Today `aggregateFor` always returns 0, so this branch never runs and nothing changes. Once aggregates become non-zero, the verdict will depend on whether an unrelated specific entry exists:
- If an ID-0 entry is present (for example, one not expanded via `AllAggregates`) and no specific entry matches, the ID-0 entry is applied.
- If any lower-precedence specific entry exists, the same ID-0 entry is ignored, even a higher-precedence deny.

The userspace test `lookup` will not reflect either case. Either drop the fallback and rely on the expansion of ID 0 into `AllAggregates`, or apply the same precedence logic in both places.

findings.title: Non-promise thenables
findings.body:
On the fast path for a thenable chunk, `next()` returns whatever `chunk.then(...)` returns. Native promises return a promise, so they work. A spec-compliant custom thenable such as `{ then(res) { res(1) } }` returns `undefined` (or any non-promise value), so `next()` stops returning a promise. `for await` then fails with "Iterator result undefined is not an object".

The old async generator awaited any thenable correctly. A fix is to wrap the call, for example `new Promise((res, rej) => then.call(chunk, res, rej))`, or to resolve the value through a native promise before chaining.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Sync throw/hang
findings.body:
This affects both the `chunk.then` getter and the `then` call itself.

- **Fast path:** if either throws, `next()` throws synchronously instead of returning a rejected promise. `inFlight` has already been set to `true`, so every later `next()`/`return()`/`throw()` is queued forever and the stream is never finalized or destroyed.
- **Waiting path (`pump()`):** the same throw happens inside a `.then` callback. It becomes an unhandled rejection, and the caller's `next()` promise never settles.

The old generator caught this in its `try` block, which set the error and destroyed the stream. The throw should be caught and routed through `settleError`/`onChunkRejected`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Multi-settling thenable
findings.body:
In `pump()`, the callbacks passed to a custom thenable are not guarded against being called more than once, or calling both fulfil and reject. A misbehaving thenable could do either.

- Each call resets `inFlight = false` and calls `drain()`. If this happens while a later request is already in flight, the serialization invariant breaks: two pumps may run at once and overwrite the shared `callback`.
- A rejection may also `finalize()` the stream after a value was already delivered.

Native promises are unaffected. Guard the callbacks with a `settled` flag.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Regression: undefined chunk
findings.body: `chunk.then` is read on any non-null chunk. An object-mode stream can legitimately yield `undefined` (e.g. `push(undefined)`), which the old generator delivered via `yield undefined`. The new code throws a `TypeError` instead. In the fast path in `next()`, this is thrown synchronously instead of returning a rejected promise. In `pump()`, it is thrown inside a `.then` callback, so `resolve`/`reject` are never called. The returned promise then hangs and `inFlight` stays `true`, blocking every later request. Guard with `chunk != null` (or similar) before reading `.then`.

In that case `next()` returns `undefined` instead of a promise, and callers get a `TypeError` on `await it.next()` or `.then`. The old generator awaited such chunks correctly. The `pump()` path handles this properly by wrapping with `resolve`/`reject`, so the fast path should do the same. For example, wrap the call in `new Promise((resolve, reject) => then.call(chunk, resolve, reject))` and then process the result.

findings.title: Null-byte check skipped
findings.body:
The fast path skips `validateArgumentNullCheck` because the real environment block cannot contain null bytes. `getEnvPairs()` uses the per-`Environment` store, though, and inside a Worker that is a `MapKVStore` (unless `SHARE_ENV` is used).

`MapKVStore::Set` keeps embedded NULs. So in a worker, `process.env.FOO = 'a\0b'` followed by `spawn(cmd)` now behaves differently:
- Before this PR, it threw `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE`.
- Now the value is passed through and silently truncated at the NUL when converted to a C string for `uv_spawn`.

A key containing a NUL is also silently dropped, because `Get(*key_utf8)` looks it up with a truncated `const char*`. The fix is to keep the null check for non-real stores, or to validate in `KVStore::Pairs`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Truncated key lookup
findings.body:
The default `KVStore::Pairs` looks up each key with `Get(*key_utf8)`, which takes a `const char*`. Any key with an embedded NUL (possible in `MapKVStore`) is therefore looked up under a truncated name. The result is either that the key is skipped, or that the value of a different key (the prefix) is emitted under the full key name.

Using the `Local<String>` `Get` overload, or a length-aware lookup, would avoid this mismatch.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Behavior change
findings.body: The default path now ignores the JS-visible `process.env` and reads the native environment store instead. `process.env` is a writable property, so code that does `process.env = { ... }` previously had its replacement object inherited by `spawn()`, because the old code spread `process.env`. After this change the child silently gets the original native environment and ignores the replacement. I am not certain how much code relies on this, but it is an observable semantic change that the PR does not mention.

findings.title: Null-byte check dropped

In a Worker without `SHARE_ENV`, `process.env` is backed by a `MapKVStore`, and the default `KVStore::Pairs()` builds pairs from those strings. Keys and values are stored with their full length, so a null byte can be present. Previously `validateArgumentNullCheck` threw `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE`. Now the pair reaches `uv_spawn()` and is silently truncated at the null byte. Whether a worker can actually store such a value depends on `MapKVStore::Set`, which I did not see in this diff.

findings.title: Possible TypeError
findings.body:
The first condition uses optional chaining (`previous?.isCJ || next?.isCJ`), so either `previous` or `next` can be undefined. The second condition then reads `previous.kind` and `next.kind` without optional chaining.

This crashes when a whitespace node sits at the start or end of a sentence next to a CJ word. Example: a text node ending in `日本語\n` followed by an inline node such as emphasis or a link. Here `previous.isCJ` is true and `next` is undefined, so `next.kind` throws.

Use `previous?.kind` and `next?.kind`, or return early when either neighbor is missing.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Guard against undefined sibling nodes
findings.body:
The first condition uses optional chaining, so it treats `previous` or `next` as possibly undefined. The second condition then reads `.kind` on both without that guard. If a whitespace node sits at the start or end of a sentence next to a CJ character, this throws a `TypeError`. Use optional chaining here too.

Improved code:
!(
  (previous?.kind === KIND_K_LETTER && next?.kind === KIND_CJ_LETTER) ||
  (next?.kind === KIND_K_LETTER && previous?.kind === KIND_CJ_LETTER)
)
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Possible Crash
findings.body:
`isLineBreakAmbiguous` guards `previous` and `next` with `?.` in the first clause. The second clause then dereferences them unguarded (`previous.kind`, `next.kind`). If `previous` or `next` is undefined while the other side is CJ, this throws a `TypeError`. For example, a whitespace node at the edge of its parent with a CJ neighbor on the other side would trigger it. Guard these accesses with `?.`.

findings.body:
The server splits the `paths` value on `,`, but commas are valid, unencoded characters in URL pathnames. `location.pathname` keeps commas as-is, for example `/tags/a,b` or `/products/1,2`. findings.title: Closing-tag regression
findings.body:
`_comment_end_re` and `_verbatim_end_re` use `[^\S\n]+`, which requires at least one whitespace character after `{%`. The old lexer compared the stripped tag content, so `{% verbatim %}x{%endverbatim%}` and `{% comment %}x{%endcomment%}` both worked.

With this change, the raw-aware splitter never finds the closing tag. The rest of the template becomes a single text token, and the parser raises an "unclosed tag" `TemplateSyntaxError`.

The behavior is also inconsistent within the PR. The opening tag is detected after `strip()`, so `{%verbatim%}` and `{%comment%}` open a raw block. The named-verbatim end regex uses `[^\S\n]*`, so it accepts `{%endverbatim name%}`. Using `*` instead of `+` in these two regexes would restore the old behavior.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Inconsistent raw detection
findings.body:
`_raw_start_re` requires whitespace after `{%` (`\s+`), but `_raw_end_tag_re` strips the content and also treats `{%comment%}` and `{%verbatim%}` as raw openers. As a result, the same template tokenizes differently depending on whether some other `{% comment ...` or `{% verbatim ...` with a space appears elsewhere.

Example: `{%comment%}{{ x }}{%endcomment%}` works on the fast path when it is the only raw tag. If the template also contains `{% verbatim %}...{% endverbatim %}`, it goes through `_tag_re_split` instead. There the `{%comment%}` block enters raw mode and cannot be closed, because of the whitespace requirement in the end regex.

The fast-path check should accept optional whitespace (`\s*`) so it matches what `_raw_end_tag_re` accepts.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.body:

Both were valid before, because the content is stripped and compared. Without a match, the rest of the template is swallowed as text and parsing fails with an unclosed-tag error. Use `*` instead of `+`, matching the named-verbatim regex.

Improved code:
_comment_end_re = re.compile(
    r"%s[^\S\n]*endcomment[^\S\n]*%s"
    % (re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START), re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_END))
)
_verbatim_end_re = re.compile(
    r"%s[^\S\n]*endverbatim[^\S\n]*%s"
    % (re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START), re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_END))
)
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Breaks async views
findings.body:
The new `wrapper` is always a plain sync function. When `non_atomic_requests` decorates an `async def` view, `iscoroutinefunction(wrapper)` returns False. Django's handler then treats the view as sync. It calls the view in a thread and gets back an un-awaited coroutine instead of an `HttpResponse`, so the request fails ("didn't return an HttpResponse object").

This is a regression, because the previous implementation returned the original view unchanged. When `iscoroutinefunction(view)` is true, the decorator should define an `async def` wrapper that awaits the view. Alternatively, it can mark the wrapper with `markcoroutinefunction`. Adding a test with an async view would catch this.

findings.body:
The array branch always writes into a freshly allocated plain `np.zeros` buffer, even when no endpoints are equal. This silently drops array subclasses and their extra state, such as masks or units, that the original `np.subtract(stop, start, ...)` preserved, so `linspace` can behave differently for subclass inputs.     delta = dt.type(0) if equal else np.subtract(
        stop, start, dtype=type(dt))
elif not equal.any():
    delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt))

    delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt), where=~equal,
                        out=np.zeros(equal.shape, dtype=type(dt)))

findings.title: Normalization bypass
findings.body:
`CollapseLeadingSlashes` runs before the code that prepends `/` to relative patterns, and it only acts when the string already starts with `/`. A pattern that starts with a backslash skips normalization, then gets `/` prepended, which recreates the scheme-relative shape.

Example: the IIS rule `url="{R:1}"` with a capture of `\example.com` (or `\\example.com`) becomes `/\example.com`. Browsers treat that as `//example.com`, so the open redirect still works. The same applies to Apache rules like `RewriteRule /legacy/(.*) $1 [R=302]`.

Fix: normalize after the leading `/` is prepended, or make the helper also collapse a leading run that begins with `\`. Add test cases where the target has no leading `/` and the capture starts with `\`.

notes: Open redirect: the fix is incomplete. Redirect targets that begin with a backslash (e.g. `\\host` or `\/host`) are not collapsed. They have `/` prepended afterwards and become `/\\host` or `/\/host`, which browsers treat as scheme-relative and so resolve off-origin.

findings.title: Stale Bounds check
findings.body:
The new "anchor at end" shortcut compares the current viewport end with `Bounds.Width`/`Bounds.Height`. During measure, `Bounds` still holds the previous arrange size, so the panel compares against the old extent.

Example scenario:
- The items source is replaced or grows a lot (say 100 → 1000 items) while the viewport sits at the old end.
- `_hasReachedEnd` is false at that point.
- `viewportEnd >= oldBounds` passes, so the anchor jumps to `itemCount - 1`.
- The scroll position snaps to the end of the new list instead of keeping the current offset.

The same stale comparison feeds `anchorAtEnd` in `RealizeElements`.

Uncertain: whether `_hasReachedEnd` is always still true in these reset or growth paths. If it is, the shortcut is skipped.

Possible fix: base the condition on the estimated or known extent for the current item count rather than the last arranged `Bounds`.

findings.title: Popup Can Go Off-Screen
findings.body:
In `Pointer` mode, once `_hasInitialPosition` is set, later size changes no longer reach the positioner. The positioner's constraint adjustments (flip/slide to stay inside screen bounds) are therefore never re-applied.

Scenario: a context flyout opens near the bottom or right screen edge, then its content grows (async items load, an expander opens). The popup keeps its original anchor and its new area extends off-screen.

The first arrange may also run before content reaches its final size. That locks in a position computed for a smaller popup.

Consider still repositioning when the new bounds would violate screen constraints, or re-running only the constraint adjustment with the original anchor point.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Ineffective Test
findings.body:
The test does not actually verify the fix.

- It asserts `PixelPoint(0,0)` both before and after the resize. The mock popup positioner may never move the window, so the test likely passes without the `PopupRoot` change.
- The raw pointer move happens after the flyout is already open. Pointer placement uses the pointer position captured when the flyout opens, so this move does not change the anchor.
- With `UseOverlayPopups`, `host` is an `OverlayPopupHost`, so `platformImpl` is null. `Assert.Equal(null, new PixelPoint())` would then fail, or the scenario is not covered at all.

Assert that the position after the resize equals the actual position captured after opening, and use a size change that would produce a different position without the fix.

findings.title: Pointer Placement Not Updated
findings.body: `_hasInitialPosition` is only reset in `Dispose()`. A `PopupRoot` that is reused across close/open cycles, or one whose `_popupPositionRequest` is updated via `ConfigurePosition` with a new pointer location while open, will never reposition because `reposition` is forced to false. Position changes from a new request (for example, re-showing a flyout at a different pointer location, or a change of anchor rect or offset) will then be ignored. The flag should be reset when the position request changes or when the popup hides.

findings.title: Wrong CommandSource
findings.body: `DeleteExpression` is now passed `CommandSource.ExecuteUpdate` instead of `CommandSource.ExecuteDelete`. Before this PR, `NonQueryExpression` set `ExecuteDelete` for delete expressions. As a result, every `ExecuteDelete`/`ExecuteDeleteAsync` call reports the wrong command source. This affects anything that reads it, such as `DbCommandInterceptor`s, diagnostic events and logging that check `CommandEventData.CommandSource`. The delete branch should use `CommandSource.ExecuteDelete`.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Use correct command source for deletes
findings.body:
The `DeleteExpression` branch passes `CommandSource.ExecuteUpdate`, so `ExecuteDelete` operations are reported with the wrong command source. The removed `NonQueryExpression` carried `CommandSource.ExecuteDelete` for deletes. Diagnostics, interceptors and logging that rely on `CommandSource` would misidentify deletes as updates; use `CommandSource.ExecuteDelete` here.

Improved code:
DeleteExpression deleteExpression => GenerateNonQueryShaper(deleteExpression.ApplyTags(_tags), CommandSource.ExecuteDelete),

findings.title: Possible Panic
findings.body:
After the pidfd reports read-readiness, the code assumes `try_wait()` always returns `Some` and calls `.expect(...)`. If it returns `Ok(None)`, user code panics inside `Child::wait()`.

The readiness is not cleared and there is no retry, so any spurious readiness or wakeup before the child is reapable will panic. This includes readiness carried over after `reregister` into a new runtime.

Instead, clear the readiness when `try_wait()` returns `None` and keep polling, rather than panicking.

findings.title: Fragile Test Helper
findings.body:
`is_pidfd_available` calls `split_once('-').unwrap()` on the `uname -r` output. Kernel release strings without a `-` (e.g. `6.6.0` on custom or vanilla builds) will panic. The tests then fail instead of running or being skipped.

Use `split(|c| c == '-' || c == '+')` or a similar approach that tolerates release strings without a suffix.

findings.title: Robust kernel version parsing in tests
findings.body:
Kernel release strings do not always contain a `-` (e.g. `6.1.0` or `6.5.0+`). In that case `split_once('-').unwrap()` panics and the tests fail instead of being skipped. Take the leading version part without assuming a dash is present.

Improved code:
let version = stdout
    .trim()
    .split(|c: char| !(c.is_ascii_digit() || c == '.'))
    .next()
    .unwrap_or("");
let mut kernel_version_iter = version.split('.');

findings.title: Possible Bug
findings.body: `Pidfd::open` treats every `pidfd_open` failure as "no pidfd support" and returns `None`, and `PidfdReaper::new` then returns `Err((None, child))`, so the caller silently falls back to the signal reaper. That fallback is reasonable for ENOSYS, but `PIDFD_NONBLOCK` is only accepted by kernels 5.10+. On kernels 5.3-5.9, `pidfd_open` fails with EINVAL on every call. The `NO_PIDFD_SUPPORT` cache is only set for ENOSYS, so each spawn repeats a failing syscall. This is only a performance cost. The cache could also cover EINVAL.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Panic Risk
findings.body: `poll` calls `.expect("pidfd is ready to read, the process should have exited")` on the result of `try_wait()`. A pidfd becomes readable when the process exits, so this is normally true. However, `Child` is publicly exposed and `try_wait`/`kill` go through `std_child()`. If a user calls `try_wait()` and reaps the child before the future is polled, the next `try_wait` in `poll` may return an error (ECHILD) or `Ok(None)`, and the `expect` panics. The semantics of the std `Child` also make `Ok(None)` possible under other conditions (e.g. spurious readiness). Returning an error or re-polling is safer than panicking.

findings.title: Fragile Error Match
findings.body: `is_rt_shutdown_err` identifies the runtime-shutdown error by comparing the deprecated `Error::description()` string to `RUNTIME_SHUTTING_DOWN_ERROR`. This is brittle: if the error is wrapped or its message changes, the `reregister` path silently stops working. A child spawned in one runtime and awaited in another will then fail with an error. The test `process_spawned_and_wait_in_different_runtime` covers this today, but the string-based coupling is fragile.

findings.title: Inverted Condition
findings.body:
The checks use `last_op_result().is_none()` on `fetch_build_data_queue` and `fetch_proc_macros_queue`. That is true only while the op has never completed, which contradicts the comment ("have finished fetching the build data once" / "finished loading the proc-macros once").

With the default config, where build scripts and proc-macro expansion are enabled:
- Before the first build-data or proc-macro load finishes, `fetch_semantic` is true. This is the case the PR is meant to prevent.
- Once each load has completed and `last_op_result()` becomes `Some`, `fetch_semantic` stays false. Semantic diagnostics are then permanently disabled for the session.

Both checks should be `last_op_result().is_some() && !op_in_progress()`.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Fix inverted readiness checks for diagnostics
findings.body:
The build-data and proc-macro checks are inverted. `last_op_result().is_none()` is true only before the first fetch has finished. Once build scripts or proc-macros load, `fetch_semantic` becomes `false` permanently, so semantic diagnostics are never computed again. The checks should instead require that a result exists, which matches the comment "have finished ... once".

Improved code:
let fetch_semantic = self.vfs_done
    && self.fetch_workspaces_queue.last_op_result().is_some()
    && (!self.config.run_build_scripts(None)
        || self.fetch_build_data_queue.last_op_result().is_some())
    && (!self.config.expand_proc_macros()
        || self.fetch_proc_macros_queue.last_op_result().is_some());
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Inverted Condition
findings.body: The comment says semantic diagnostics should wait until build data and proc-macros have finished loading once. The code instead requires `last_op_result().is_none()` on both `fetch_build_data_queue` and `fetch_proc_macros_queue`. That is true only while no operation has ever completed, and false once one has. If `last_op_result()` returns `Some` after a completed fetch, as it does for `fetch_workspaces_queue` above, semantic diagnostics are enabled before loading starts and disabled once it finishes. That is the opposite of the intended behavior. It likely should be `.is_some()`. I could not confirm what the queue's output type returns for a completed run, so this is worth checking.

findings.title: Fix inverted readiness check for diagnostics
findings.body:
The condition is inverted. `last_op_result().is_none()` means the operation has never completed, so semantic diagnostics are enabled only while build data and proc-macros are not loaded. Once they finish (`is_some()`), diagnostics are disabled permanently. Require `is_some()` and `!op_in_progress()` instead.

Improved code:
&& (!self.config.run_build_scripts(None)
    || (self.fetch_build_data_queue.last_op_result().is_some()
        && !self.fetch_build_data_queue.op_in_progress()))
&& (!self.config.expand_proc_macros()
    || (self.fetch_proc_macros_queue.last_op_result().is_some()
        && !self.fetch_proc_macros_queue.op_in_progress()));

findings.title: Fragile Error Matching
findings.body: `isResourceQuotaConflict` identifies retryable errors by matching two substrings in the error message. If the API server wording changes, or the error is wrapped or localized, the retry silently stops working and the original failure returns with no diagnostic. A structured check would be more robust, for example `StatusError.Status().Details.Kind == "resourcequotas"`. The `Details` field is populated for these conflicts, so it may be a better fit. The message match could stay as a fallback. This is a robustness concern rather than a confirmed bug, because the current message format is stable today.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Stale dispatcher returned
findings.body:
Updates are silently lost if `globalThis` is frozen after the global dispatcher symbol already exists.

This happens in the common case: undici, or Node's bundled fetch, sets the dispatcher first, and the app calls `Object.freeze(globalThis)` later. Freezing makes the existing property non-writable, so a later `setGlobalDispatcher(newAgent)` fails in `defineProperty`. The `TypeError` is caught and `newAgent` goes into `fallbackDispatcher`.

However, `getGlobalDispatcher` returns `globalThis[globalDispatcher] ?? fallbackDispatcher`. The global property is still the old agent, so the fallback is never read. The call appears to succeed but has no effect, and requests keep using the old agent.

Fix options:
- Have `getGlobalDispatcher` prefer `fallbackDispatcher` once it is set.
- Or clear `fallbackDispatcher` on a successful define and check it first.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Stale Dispatcher
findings.body: If undici is loaded first and `globalThis` is frozen afterwards, `setGlobalDispatcher` silently stops working. This is the usual `Object.freeze(globalThis)` ordering. The existing `globalDispatcher` property becomes non-writable and non-configurable. Redefining it with a new value throws a `TypeError`, which the catch block swallows after storing the agent in `fallbackDispatcher`. `getGlobalDispatcher` then returns `globalThis[globalDispatcher] ?? fallbackDispatcher`. The old value is non-nullish, so the stale dispatcher is returned and the new one is never used, with no error. The fallback should take precedence once it has been set, or `getGlobalDispatcher` should check `fallbackDispatcher` first.

findings.title: Silent stale session
findings.body: `cached_db` reads from the cache before the database. If the cache delete fails, the DB row is gone but the cached session data stays valid until the cache entry expires. Before this change, the exception made `delete()` and `flush()` (used by `logout()`) fail visibly. Now logout looks successful while a copy of the session cookie can still authenticate until cache expiry. Swallowing errors is fine for `save()`, but for `delete()` it is a security trade-off. Consider documenting this explicitly, or retrying or invalidating the entry another way (e.g. setting a short-lived tombstone).
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Docs formatting
findings.body: The `versionchanged` body is indented with 2 spaces, but Django docs use 4 spaces for directive content. The sentence "only failed writes were caught and logged rather than failed deletes" also reads awkwardly. Suggested wording: "In older versions, exceptions raised when deleting from the cache weren't handled." A release note entry for 6.2 also seems to be missing.
findings.label: nit

notes: Incomplete session invalidation: when the cache delete fails, the exception is now only logged. The session remains readable from the cache (which `cached_db` checks first) even though the database row was deleted. A logged-out or flushed session can therefore keep working until the cache entry expires, and the user is not shown any error. The stale cache entry also existed before this PR; the new part is that the failure is no longer surfaced to the caller.

findings.title: Failed cache delete can leave stale session
findings.label: invalid

notes: Stale session after failed cache delete: if `cache.delete()` fails, the session is removed from the DB but its cached copy remains. `load()` reads the cache first, so the session can stay valid after logout or flush until the cache entry expires. Previously the exception propagated and the failure was visible to the caller. Now it is only logged. This appears to be the intended trade-off for this ticket, so I flag it only as a behavioral note. Operators should monitor the new log message.

findings.title: Deferred update dropped
findings.body: `_hasDeferredDynamicOverflowUpdate` is only consumed inside the `if (_overflowPopup != null)` block of the `IsOpen` handler. If an update is requested while `_isOpeningOverflowPopup` is true, the flag is set and then applied right after. It is never cleared or applied on other paths, so a stale flag could trigger an extra update later. This is low risk because the flag is only set while `_isOpeningOverflowPopup` is true, which only happens inside that block. The remaining uncertainty is whether setting `_overflowPopup.IsOpen = true` can throw. In that case the `finally` resets `_isOpeningOverflowPopup`, but the deferred flag stays set and is applied only on the next open.
